title: Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab
gist: A sponsored ServeTheHome tour of AWS's networking lab shows in-house switches spanning 3.2 Tbps to 102.4 Tbps, a line-rate encrypting switch, custom management hardware and a separate timing network with 20-microsecond accuracy. The collected text ends before the optics, connectors and hollow-core fiber sections, which are covered only in the intro summary.

insights.claim: AWS designs its own switch family spanning 3.2 Tbps (32 ports of 100GbE QSFP28), 12.8 Tbps (400G QSFP-DD, the current volume deployment), 51.2 Tbps (800GbE OSFP) and 102.4 Tbps (1.6T OSFP).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AWS's vertically integrated switch cadence is a read-through for demand for 800G and 1.6T optics and high-speed SerDes.

insights.claim: AWS is deploying its 51.2 Tbps generation heavily at the time of filming, with OSFP ports running PAM4-112 SerDes for 800GbE per port.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: 800G is the mainstream hyperscale deployment speed now, which supports 800G optics demand.
insights.quote: AWS is deploying the 51.2 Tbps generation heavily at the time of filming.

insights.claim: AWS's 102.4 Tbps switch uses PAM4-224 SerDes for 1.6 Tbps per OSFP port, is not yet in volume deployment, and is to roll out over the coming quarters and years.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 1.6T ramp at AWS would be a timing marker for 224G SerDes and 1.6T optical module volume.

insights.claim: At 1.6T port speeds, AWS's optical modules include their own built-in cooling, and the switch is 16 times the per-port bandwidth of the 3.2 Tbps design on twice as many ports, so cooling grows accordingly.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Thermal and power design is becoming a primary constraint and differentiator in next-generation switch and optics hardware.
insights.locator: Each OSFP port uses PAM4-224 SerDes

insights.claim: The 12.8 Tbps generation was when AWS moved signaling from NRZ to PAM4, and each newer switch needs bigger heatsinks as power rises.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signaling transitions mark generational shifts in switch and optics supply chains.
insights.locator: The green box next to it

insights.claim: AWS switches use Annapurna Labs management processors and a logging SSD, showing AWS applies its own silicon beyond compute into networking management.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AWS in-house silicon extends across the stack, reducing merchant-silicon content in management functions.
insights.locator: Inside there is an Annapurna Labs management processor

insights.claim: AWS considers a small internal board that polls every pluggable optic over I2C for telemetry a major innovation, since it lets operators identify a failing module before it affects its neighbors.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Optics failure is a key operational risk at scale, and telemetry-based prediction is a differentiator for hyperscalers.
insights.locator: A small board with a big job

insights.claim: AWS builds its own 1GbE management switch and serial console server because the management plane is what makes a large network operable at its scale, using the same architecture as its high-speed boxes.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers vertically integrate even low-end networking, limiting the addressable market for merchant management switches.

themes.theme: Encryption and long-haul in the switch

insights.claim: AWS has a 12.8 Tbps switch that encrypts every port using sixteen FPGAs, on the reasoning that data leaving a data center should be encrypted by default, and its ports accept high-power 400ZR optics so it can also serve as long-haul equipment.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Line-rate encryption plus coherent optics in a single box shows convergence of switching and DCI, relevant to 400ZR demand and FPGA usage.
insights.quote: data leaving a data center should be encrypted by default

insights.claim: AWS keeps time across fleets of hundreds of thousands of servers with satellite-referenced timing appliances distributing a pulse-per-second signal over a dedicated, proprietary timing network separate from its data and management networks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Precise timing infrastructure is a hyperscaler differentiator supporting distributed databases and could create demand for timing silicon.

insights.claim: AWS claims its timing infrastructure guarantees time within 20 microseconds, versus roughly 500 microseconds for standard NTP, and says the figure is conservative.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 25x accuracy advantage over NTP supports stronger consistency guarantees in AWS distributed services.
insights.quote: AWS claims its timing infrastructure guarantees time to within 20 microseconds

insights.claim: Distributed databases need accurate write timestamps so reads return current data, and log analysis is only as reliable as its clock sources, which is why accurate time matters for ordering.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Timing accuracy underpins database consistency, making it a cloud-service competitive feature.

insights.claim: AWS's timing appliance is built as a tree with four upstream ports and the rest downstream, calibrated using a map of the tree with cable lengths and speeds, and uses two FPGAs for pluggable monitoring and a third for proprietary timing logic.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Custom timing hardware relies on FPGAs, a use case outside mainstream AI accelerators.
insights.locator: The front panel resembles a 48-port SFP switch

insights.claim: AWS's lab also develops DWDM modules that put 64 wavelengths on one fiber strand, hollow-core fiber with roughly 33 percent better latency, and connectors that install 64 fibers in about one second; the article body collected here does not detail these.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hollow-core fiber and dense DWDM are directions hyperscalers are pursuing for latency and fiber efficiency.
insights.quote: DWDM modules that put 64 wavelengths on one fiber strand, hollow-core fiber with roughly 33 percent better latency
insights.locator: AWS invited us to tour the networking lab

insights.claim: The tour was sponsored with AWS covering travel, and AWS reviewed the footage so only approved frames are used, which means disclosures were controlled by AWS.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Treat details as AWS-curated disclosure rather than independent verification.
insights.locator: Since Sam and I had to fly to the lab
